text: Now a full verification comparing every key (type, value, TTL, stream groups):

I copied all the data to the new Valkey server and made it a standalone primary that accepts writes. A key-by-key check found no differences.

**How I copied it**
1. I pointed Valkey (port 6380) at the Redis server (port 6379) as a replica, so it pulled a full copy of the data in one go. All 3,270 keys loaded (2,920 in db0 and 350 in db2) and none had expired.
2. Once both servers were at the same point in the data, I disconnected Valkey from Redis. It now runs on its own as a primary. A test write and delete on it worked.

**Check results**
I ran a script that went through all 16 databases on both servers and compared every key. All 3,270 matched with 0 differences:
- **Keys and types:** the same set of keys exists in each database, with the same types.
- **Values:** every value matches, compared in the way that suits each type.
- **Time to live:** the same keys have an expiry, and the remaining times differ by under 5 seconds (the time between the two checks).
- **Streams:** entries, last ID, consumer groups (including the last message each group has received), consumer names and pending messages all match.

**Things to know**
- **Old server:** Redis is still running, and its data was only read, never changed. The one side effect is that serving the copy created a small replication buffer in its memory. It is harmless, and Redis now reports no connected replicas.
- **Restarts:** I did not edit `/etc/valkey/valkey.conf`. It contains no setting that would make Valkey copy from Redis again, so Valkey will start as a primary after a restart. That file has no `save` lines, so Valkey uses its default schedule for saving data to disk. Unless something overrides that default, the copied data will survive a restart.

The check script is at `/tmp/verify.py` if you want to run it again.
